19957-facing-the-german-foe:
Colonel James Fiske titled his boys' war book Facing the German Foe in 1915. A young recruit marvels that his new comrades speak his language. You do say some funny things, though, old chap, he admits. Mr. Grenfel let him join the troop right away, to his surprise. The scene is a British troop welcoming an American boy. Fiske wrote the Great War for young readers while it raged.

America was neutral in 1915, but its boys read war hungrily. Fiske's series put American youths inside the Allied armies. Language jokes ease the plunge into trenches. The foe of the title is faced early and often. Such books shaped a generation's war imagination. They are period pieces of mobilized boyhood.
20744-mary-s-peake-the-colored-teacher-a:
Mary S. Peake taught freed children at Fortress Monroe during the Civil War, and this short life tells her story. Her uncle John Paine was freed by a kind man who bought slaves to set them free. Mary grew up as a pet of that household, treated almost like a daughter.

Peake's school work under Union guns made her a famed figure in Black education. The book keeps her faith, care, and early death before the reader. It is brief, but it kept her name alive when few Black teachers were honored in print. Readers meet a quiet hero of the war years.
21787-shelled-by-an-unseen-foe:
Boys at a military school feel the pull of the Great War in this 1916 novel by Colonel James Fiske. It is volume eight of the World's War Series. The tallest of three friends announces that he is going home. Ripping times are promised there. His father and brothers are already in the field, and one brother was shot in the trenches in France.

The chapters carry the young men from school into service, through struggle, letters home, and days of waiting. A bit of romance and a girl named Helen soften the war's edge. Fiske wrote while the war still raged, for boys who expected to follow. It is a period piece of wartime youth fiction, earnest and brisk.
22347-through-canal-land-in-a-canadian-c:
Through Canal Land in a Canadian Canoe follows a pleasure trip by water. The travelers spent three weeks on their planned route. The day fixed for the start found them in high spirits.

All arrangements stood complete when that morning came. The party overflowed with cheerful hopes for the good time ahead. Health and spirits, the account says, were at their best. Canal travel by canoe mixed ease with slow adventure. Such trips let holiday makers see country from its waterways. Readers get a cheerful period travel record. It recalls a time when three free weeks and a canoe promised a complete escape.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antinoe: A 1913 entry on Antinoe — Antinoöpolis, the Egyptian city, now a titular see. Henri Leclercq tells its Christian past. Its bishops graced the old councils. The Nile guards its ruined quays. A see of the Thebaid. Its bishops signed the ancient creeds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arsinoe: A 1913 entry on Arsinoe — the Egyptian city, now a titular see. Thomas Shahan notes its Christian past. Its bishops graced the old councils. The Faiyum guards its ruined site. A see of the Nile's valley. Its bishops signed the ancient creeds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartholomew-r: This 1913 reference piece on Bartholomew Roe — the Benedictine martyr. John Wainewright honors his death. He died for the old faith's sake. The entry preserves his modest fame. A monk of the English martyrs. His death honored the Benedictine habit. His feast joins the martyrs' roll.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caloe: This 1913 reference piece presents Caloe — a Lydian city, now a titular see. Pétridès sums up its Christian past. Old records name its bishops. The Church keeps the old title. It lay in the Asian valleys. The Maeander watered its plain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-monroe: A 1913 entry on Monroe — the fifth president. Thomas Meehan notes his famous doctrine. His pen warned the European crowns. The nation bless the prudent name. The era of good feelings crowned his rule. His 1831 death is famed. His 1831 doctrine is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kerry-and-agh: This 1913 reference piece on Kerry and Aghadoe — the Irish diocese. Denis O'Connor gives its ancient story. Its bishops guard the southwestern flock. The entry keeps its modest record. A see of the Erin's west. Its ancient see is famed. Its bishops are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-killaloe: A 1913 entry on Killaloe — the Irish diocese. Michael Breen gives its ancient story. Its bishops guard the Shannon flock. The entry keeps its modest record. A see of the Erin's west. Its ancient see is famed. Its bishops are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-linoe: A 1913 entry on Linoe — a vanished Bithynian see. Sophrone Pétridès recounts its ruined history. Bishops once guided the local flock. Few documents recall its past. The Church now ranks it titular. Its vanished bishops are famed. Its titular dignity is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrick-donah: Patrick Donahoe was the Boston publisher whose Pilot served Irish America for generations. This entry covers his career, his newspaper, and his influence. The voice of Irish Boston: his faithful Pilot guided Boston's Irish immigrants faithfully for many long decades.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raphoe: Raphoe became the diocese of Donegal's Catholics. This entry covers its bishops, churches, and history. The faith in the hills of Tyrconnell: its small cathedral serves Donegal's faithful in Letterkenny town today in prayer and song and living faith and hope.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-siloe: Siloe was the pool of the blind man's washing. This entry examines its waters, its tunnel, and its Gospel. The fountain of the Jerusalem valley: its cool waters healed the blind in the Gospel of John's ninth chapter in the Bible.
first-project-gutenberg-collection-of-ed: A gathering of Poe's essential work: "The Raven," "Annabel Lee," "The Tell-Tale Heart," "The Fall of the House of Usher," and more poems and tales. In one volume, the inventor of the detective story and the master of American dread. The perfect introduction to a genius of the macabre.
grand-ther-baldwin-s-thanksgiving-with-o: Horatio Alger's ballads and poems, including the Thanksgiving piece of the title. Sentimental, moral, and rhythmic, they show the other side of the rags-to-riches author. Verse for young readers of the 1870s. Alger's verse is as earnest and moral as his famous stories.
podcast-joerogan-l_Y3tUZRvOE:
Jimmy Corsetti joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 1742. Corsetti's Bright Insight channel turned him into the internet's history hunter, arguing for lost chapters of the human past. His specialty is Atlantis and the sites he says the experts misread.

He walks Rogan through the evidence he rates highest, from the Sahara's Richat Structure to drowned coasts and old maps. Rogan asks how a YouTube researcher checks himself without a university behind him. The episode is a full hearing for the amateur's case, in a studio that has done more than any other to amplify it.
the-further-adventures-of-robinson-cruso: Defoe's 1719 sequel sends Crusoe back to his island colony, which has fallen into quarreling and disorder, and then onward to adventures across Asia and Siberia. Less famous than the original, it is still packed with shipwrecks, captivity, and narrow escapes. Readers who want more of literature's most famous castaway will find Crusoe older, wearier, and still impossible to keep off the sea.
